hint: It is a zero-over-zero form; differentiate top and bottom and use the parity of m times N minus one.

question: The instantaneous intensity of an electric field is $I = \gamma E^{2}$, with $\gamma$ a known constant. Using the mode-locked field $E_{\rm after}(t) = E_{0}\cos(\omega_{0}t)\,\dfrac{\sin(N\Delta\omega\,t/2)}{\sin(\Delta\omega\,t/2)}$, write down the total instantaneous intensity $I_{\rm after}(t)$.
solution: Square the field: $I_{\rm after}(t) = \gamma E_{0}^{2}\cos^{2}(\omega_{0}t)\left[\frac{\sin(N\Delta\omega t/2)}{\sin(\Delta\omega t/2)}\right]^{2}$. The intensity factors into a fast optical oscillation $\cos^{2}(\omega_{0}t)$ and a slow envelope $\left[\sin(N\Delta\omega t/2)/\sin(\Delta\omega t/2)\right]^{2}$ that rises to $N^{2}$ once per round-trip time $2\pi/\Delta\omega$ and stays small in between. The mode-locked laser therefore emits a train of short, intense bursts rather than steady light.
hint: Square the field expression; the result separates into a fast carrier factor times a slow envelope factor.

question: For the mode-locked intensity $I_{\rm after}(t) = \gamma E_{0}^{2}\cos^{2}(\omega_{0}t)\left[\frac{\sin(N\Delta\omega\,t/2)}{\sin(\Delta\omega\,t/2)}\right]^{2}$, where the carrier coincides with a cavity mode ($\omega_{0} = m\,\Delta\omega$, $m$ an integer), find the maximum possible intensity of the total field and the time(s) at which it is achieved.
solution: The envelope peaks where $\Delta\omega\,t/2$ is an integer multiple of $\pi$: both sine and cosine of the ratio vanish there, and by the limit of part (c) the ratio tends to $N$, so the envelope reaches $N^{2}$. This occurs at $\Delta\omega\,t = 2\pi k$, i.e. $t = 2\pi k/\Delta\omega$ — the cavity round-trip times. At those instants the carrier contributes $\cos^{2}(\omega_{0}t) = \cos^{2}(2\pi km) = 1$ because $\omega_{0}/\Delta\omega = m$ is an integer, so carrier and envelope peak together. Hence $I_{\max} = \gamma N^{2}E_{0}^{2}$ at $t = 2\pi k/\Delta\omega$; compared with $N$ incoherent modes (intensity of order $\gamma NE_{0}^{2}$), locking compresses the same energy into pulses about $N$ times more intense.
hint: Maximize the envelope using the limit from part (c), then verify the carrier factor is also maximal at those instants.

question: A robot eye images a printed page with a circular pupil (aperture) of diameter $d = 5.00\ \mathrm{mm}$, the page held at distance $L = 25.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ in front of the pupil, using light of wavelength $\lambda = 550\ \mathrm{nm}$. Diffraction at the circular pupil limits the angular resolution to the Rayleigh angle $\theta_{\min} = 1.22\,\lambda/d$: two dots on the page can just be distinguished if their angular separation exceeds $\theta_{\min}$. Estimate the diffraction-limited maximum print resolution, in dots per inch (dpi), for viewing this page.
solution: The Rayleigh criterion for a circular aperture of diameter $d$ gives a minimum resolvable angular separation $\theta_{\min} = 1.22\lambda/d$. With $\lambda = 550\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $d = 5.00\ \mathrm{mm}$: $\theta_{\min} = 1.22(550\times10^{-9})/(5.00\times10^{-3}) = 1.34\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad}$. At distance $L = 0.250\ \mathrm{m}$ this corresponds to a minimum center-to-center dot spacing $\Delta x = L\theta_{\min} = 0.250 \times 1.34\times10^{-4} = 3.36\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m} = 33.6\ \mu\mathrm{m}$. One inch is $0.0254\ \mathrm{m}$, so the number of resolvable dots per inch is $0.0254/\Delta x \approx 7.6\times10^{2}$ dpi. Order-of-magnitude check: an angle of $10^{-4}$ rad at $0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ gives tens of microns, i.e. hundreds of dpi, far finer than typical print, so ordinary vision is not diffraction-limited.
hint: Turn the Rayleigh diffraction angle into a smallest dot spacing on the page, then ask how many such spacings fit in one inch.

question: A robot eye views a stellar object (effectively at infinity); its thin lens is set so the image forms on the sensor, a distance $s_i = 10.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ behind the pupil of diameter $d = 5.00\ \mathrm{mm}$. The total optical power collected by the pupil is $P_0$. Diffraction at the circular pupil spreads the image into an Airy pattern: a central bright spot whose angular radius is $1.22\lambda/d$, with wavelength $\lambda = 550\ \mathrm{nm}$. (i) Estimate the intensity at the sensor in terms of $P_0$, $\lambda$, and the parameters of the eye ($d$, $s_i$), and give the numerical coefficient.
solution: Diffraction by a circular aperture of diameter $d$ concentrates a point source into an Airy disk of angular radius $1.22\lambda/d$; at image distance $s_i$ its linear radius is $r_{\mathrm{A}} = 1.22\,\lambda s_i/d$. Essentially all of the collected power $P_0$ lands within (roughly) this disk, so the intensity is $I \approx \dfrac{P_0}{\pi r_{\mathrm{A}}^2} = \dfrac{P_0 d^2}{\pi (1.22\,\lambda s_i)^2}$. Numerically, $r_{\mathrm{A}} = 1.22 \times 550\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m} \times 0.100/5.00\times10^{-3} = 1.34\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m}$, so $\pi r_{\mathrm{A}}^2 = 5.7\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and $I \approx 1.8\times10^{9}\,P_0\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$. Sanity check: the spot area $\pi r_{\mathrm{A}}^2 \approx 5.7\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ is about $3\times10^4$ times smaller than the pupil area $\pi(d/2)^2 \approx 2.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, consistent with a diffraction-limited concentration of the collected power.
hint: Spread the collected power over the Airy disk whose radius follows from the diffraction angle $1.22\lambda/d$ at the image distance.

question: For the diffraction-limited stellar image of the previous part, the intensity at the sensor was estimated as $I \approx P_0 d^2/\left[\pi(1.22\,\lambda s_i)^2\right]$, where $P_0$ is the power collected by a pupil of diameter $d$ and the Airy spot radius is $r_{\mathrm{A}} = 1.22\lambda s_i/d$. While observing the same star (same surface brightness, so the collected power scales with pupil area), the pupil diameter is reduced from $5.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ to $2.0\ \mathrm{mm}$. (ii) By what factor does the intensity at the sensor change?
answer: $I \propto d^4$, so $I_{\mathrm{new}}/I_{\mathrm{old}} = (2/5)^4 = 16/625 \approx 0.026$ (a decrease by a factor of $\approx 39$)
solution: Two effects combine. First, for the same object brightness the collected power scales with pupil area: $P_0 \propto d^2$. Second, the diffraction spot radius $r_{\mathrm{A}} = 1.22\lambda s_i/d$ grows as $1/d$, so the spot area $\pi r_{\mathrm{A}}^2$ scales as $1/d^2$. Hence $I \sim P_0/(\pi r_{\mathrm{A}}^2) \propto d^2 \times d^2 = d^4$. Shrinking the pupil from $d_1 = 5.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ to $d_2 = 2.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ gives $I_2/I_1 = (d_2/d_1)^4 = (2/5)^4 = 16/625 \approx 0.026$, i.e. the intensity drops by a factor $625/16 \approx 39$. Limiting check: closing the aperture entirely ($d \to 0$) must kill the signal, and the $d^4$ law indeed vanishes fastest.
hint: Both the collected power and the spot area change when the pupil shrinks; combine the two scalings.

question: We have some identical hemispherical water droplets (flat face down) whose total mass is 10 g. The droplets are subjected to a radiation of heat flux $5\times10^4\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$ incident perpendicular to their (curved) surfaces, and starting at $30^\circ\mathrm{C}$ it takes them one minute to vaporize completely. Considering only radiative transmission of heat (no conduction or convection), how many water droplets were there? (Give the nearest integer for a fractional result.) Specific heat of water $c = 4.2\ \mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$, latent heat of evaporation $L = 2257\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}$.
solution: Per kilogram, heating from $30^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to boiling and vaporizing needs $c\Delta T + L = 4.2\times 70 + 2257 = 2551$ kJ. For a droplet of radius $r$: mass $m_d = \rho\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$ and absorbed power $P = q\,(2\pi r^2)$ (flux normal to every curved-surface element). Vaporizing in $t = 60$ s requires $\rho\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3 (2.551\times10^6) = 60\times 5\times10^4 \times 2\pi r^2$, which fixes the radius: $r = \frac{120\,q}{(2/3)\rho(c\Delta T+L)} \approx 3.53$ mm. Then $m_d = \frac{2}{3}\pi(1000)(3.53\times10^{-3})^3 \approx 9.2\times10^{-5}$ kg $= 0.092$ g, so $N = 10/0.092 \approx 108.7 \approx 109$ droplets.
hint: The per-droplet energy balance (mass times specific heat + latent heat = flux times curved area times 60 s) fixes the radius; then divide 10 g by one droplet's mass.

question: Find the efficiency (energy returned on energy invested - ERoEI) of storing energy in the form of compressed air. Surplus electrical energy compresses air adiabatically from state $(P_1, V_1, T_1)$ to volume $V_2$, a compression ratio $r = V_1/V_2$. To get the energy back, the air first cools at constant volume to the temperature $T_1$ it had before compression, then expands adiabatically until its pressure returns to the original value $P_1$. Treat air as a diatomic ideal gas ($\gamma = 7/5$). State your answer as a percentage, in terms of $r$.
solution: Adiabatic compression: $T_2 = T_1 r^{\gamma-1}$ and $W_{in} = nC_v(T_2-T_1) = nC_vT_1(r^{\gamma-1}-1)$. The constant-volume cooling rejects $nC_v(T_2-T_1)$ to the environment - this heat is wasted. State 3 is $(P_1 r, V_2, T_1)$; expanding adiabatically to $P_4 = P_1$ gives $P_3V_2^\gamma = P_1V_4^\gamma \Rightarrow V_4 = V_1 r^{(1-\gamma)/\gamma}$ and $T_4 = T_1 r^{-(\gamma-1)/\gamma}$. Work returned: $W_{out} = nC_v(T_1-T_4) = nC_vT_1(1 - r^{-(\gamma-1)/\gamma})$. Hence $\eta = \frac{W_{out}}{W_{in}} = \frac{1 - r^{-(\gamma-1)/\gamma}}{r^{\gamma-1}-1}$, i.e. with $\gamma = 7/5$, $\eta = \frac{1 - r^{-2/7}}{r^{2/5}-1}$ (about 32% for $r = 10$).
hint: Adiabats give $T_2 = T_1 r^{\gamma-1}$ and $T_4 = T_1 r^{-(\gamma-1)/\gamma}$; the heat rejected during cooling is lost, so the efficiency is below 1.

question: In a certain process, the absolute temperature $T$ of an ideal gas is inversely proportional to the applied pressure $P$ (i.e. $T = C/P$ with $C$ constant). The gas has $n$ moles and starts in the state $(P_1, V_1, T_1)$. Find an expression for the work done by the gas in this process when its volume is doubled.
solution: Combine the process condition with the ideal-gas law $PV = nRT$: since $T = C/P$, we get $P^2V = nRC = \text{const} = P_1^2V_1$, so along the path $P = P_1\sqrt{V_1/V}$. The work done by the gas from $V_1$ to $2V_1$ is $W = \int_{V_1}^{2V_1} P\,dV = P_1\sqrt{V_1}\left[2\sqrt{V}\right]_{V_1}^{2V_1} = 2P_1\sqrt{V_1}\left(\sqrt{2V_1} - \sqrt{V_1}\right) = 2P_1V_1(\sqrt{2}-1)$. Since $P_1V_1 = nRT_1$, this is $W = 2nRT_1(\sqrt{2}-1) \approx 0.83\,nRT_1$, positive because the gas expands.
hint: Rewrite the condition as $P^2V = \text{const}$ using $PV = nRT$, then integrate $P\,dV$ between $V_1$ and $2V_1$.

question: In a parallel universe, when the temperature of an ideal gas falls by $7\,^\circ\text{C}$, the volume of the gas decreases by $\frac{1}{7}$ of its value at $0\,^\circ\text{C}$, the pressure being held fixed (linear volume-temperature behaviour, as in Charles's law). Let $V_0$ be the volume of the gas at $0\,^\circ\text{C}$. Find the absolute zero of temperature of that universe on the Celsius scale.
solution: By Charles's-law behaviour the volume depends linearly on the Celsius temperature, decreasing by $\frac{V_0}{7}$ for every $7\,^\circ\text{C}$ of cooling, i.e. by $\frac{V_0}{49}$ per degree. Hence $V(T) = V_0\left(1 + \frac{T}{49}\right)$ with $T$ in °C. Absolute zero is the temperature at which the extrapolated volume of the ideal gas vanishes: $V = 0 \Rightarrow T = -49\,^\circ\text{C}$. This exactly mirrors our own universe, where the volume drops by $\frac{1}{273}$ of $V_0$ per $1\,^\circ\text{C}$ and absolute zero is $-273\,^\circ\text{C}$; the constant in $V = V_0(1 + T/T_0)$ is the negative of the absolute zero on the Celsius scale.
hint: Extrapolate the linear law $V = V_0(1 + T/T_0)$ to $V = 0$.

question: Two bodies A and B have constant heat capacities $C_A$ and $C_B$ and are kept at temperatures $T_A$ and $T_B$ (Kelvin), with $T_A > T_B$. The engineer first simply puts the two bodies in direct thermal contact and lets them equilibrate. How much work is extracted during this process?
answer: 0 J (no work can be extracted from direct contact)
solution: When the bodies touch, heat flows spontaneously from the hotter body A to the colder body B by conduction. This is a purely irreversible process: the temperature difference degrades into heat flow with no mechanism arranged to raise a weight, turn a shaft, or drive a piston. The first law still holds — the energy leaving A as heat enters B as heat — but none of it is converted to work. Hence the extracted work is exactly $W = 0$. The lesson is that a temperature difference alone is not enough; you need an engine operating reversibly between the two reservoirs to convert heat flow into work, which is what parts (b) and (c) explore.
hint: Heat flowing through direct conduction performs no work; only an engine between the bodies can extract work.

question: Two bodies A and B with heat capacities $C_A$ and $C_B$ are at temperatures $T_A > T_B$. Instead of putting them in direct contact, what is the best method to extract the maximum possible work from this pair of bodies?
answer: Run a reversible (Carnot) engine between the two bodies in infinitesimal steps until they reach a common final temperature; the instantaneous efficiency is η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot
solution: Maximum work requires zero net entropy production, i.e. a fully reversible process. So the engineer should never let the bodies touch directly; instead a Carnot (reversible) engine should be operated between them: it draws heat $δQ$ from the hotter body at its current temperature $T_h$, converts the maximum fraction $1 - T_c/T_h$ into work, and dumps the rest into the colder body at $T_c$, with both heat exchanges occurring across infinitesimally small temperature differences. As the bodies gradually equilibrate, $T_h$ falls and $T_c$ rises, so the efficiency decreases steadily, and the engine stops (produces no more work) when both bodies reach the same final temperature $T_f$. No other protocol can extract more work, because any irreversibility creates entropy and wastes temperature difference.
hint: No entropy may be produced if the extracted work is to be maximal — operate a Carnot engine between the slowly changing bodies.

question: For the reversible engine operating between bodies A and B (heat capacities $C_A$, $C_B$; initial temperatures $T_A > T_B$), find the value of the parameter — the final common temperature $T_f$ — that guarantees the extracted work is indeed maximum, and write the maximum work.
answer: T_f = T_A^(C_A/(C_A+C_B)) · T_B^(C_B/(C_A+C_B)); W_max = C_AT_A + C_BT_B − (C_A + C_B)T_f
solution: In the reversible run the total entropy change of the two bodies must be zero: $ΔS = C_A ln(T_f/T_A) + C_B ln(T_f/T_B) = 0$. Rearranging, $(C_A + C_B) lnT_f = C_A lnT_A + C_B lnT_B$, so the required parameter is the heat-capacity-weighted geometric mean $T_f = T_A^{C_A/(C_A+C_B)}·T_B^{C_B/(C_A+C_B)}$. Energy conservation then gives the maximum work: $W_{max} = C_A(T_A - T_f) + C_B(T_B - T_f) = (C_AT_A + C_BT_B) - (C_A + C_B)T_f$. For comparison, direct contact would produce the arithmetic-mean final temperature $(C_AT_A + C_BT_B)/(C_A+C_B) ≥ T_f$ and zero work; any irreversibility pushes the final temperature above the geometric mean and yields less work, so this $T_f$ indeed guarantees maximality.
hint: Set the total entropy change of the two bodies to zero (reversible operation) and solve for the final temperature.

question: Neutrons in a nuclear reactor are in thermal equilibrium at temperature $T$ and obey the Maxwell speed distribution $f(v) = 4πN (m/(2πk_BT))^{3/2} v^2 e^{-mv^2/(2k_BT)}$, where $N$ is the total number of neutrons, $m$ the neutron mass and $k_B$ Boltzmann's constant, so that $f(v)dv$ is the number of neutrons with speeds between $v$ and $v + dv$. For what speed $v_p$ is $f(v)$ highest (the most probable speed)?
solution: Maximize $f(v)$ by setting $df/dv = 0$. It is easiest to maximize $ln f = const + 2 ln v - mv^2/(2k_BT)$, since the logarithm is monotonic and the constants drop out. Differentiating: $d(ln f)/dv = 2/v - mv/(k_BT) = 0$, which gives $v_p^2 = 2k_BT/m$, i.e. $v_p = √(2k_BT/m)$. The second derivative $-2/v^2 - m/(k_BT)$ is negative at that point, confirming a genuine maximum. Physically the competition is between the $v^2$ phase-space factor (favoring large speeds) and the Boltzmann exponential (favoring small speeds). For reactor neutrons thermalized in water at room temperature this most probable speed is about 2.5 km/s.
hint: Set d(ln f)/dv = 0, i.e. maximize 2 ln v − mv²/(2k_BT).

question: An ideal gas obeys $PV = nRT$, where $P$, $V$ and $T$ are the pressure, volume and temperature of the (fixed) amount $n$ of gas. For this gas kept at the definite temperature $T = 30^\circ\mathrm{C}$, what graph is obtained when the pressure $P$ is plotted along the Y-axis against the product $PV$ along the X-axis? Describe the curve and state its equation/position.
answer: A vertical straight line at $PV = nRT = 303\,nR \approx 2519\,n$ J
solution: First convert the temperature: $T = 30 + 273 = 303\,\mathrm{K}$. The ideal-gas law pins down the product for the fixed sample: $PV = nRT = 303\,nR$ (about $2.52\times10^3\,n$ joules), independent of $P$ and $V$ separately. Hence the x-coordinate $x = PV$ of every allowed state is the same constant, while $P = nRT/V$ can take any positive value as $V$ changes (halving $V$ doubles $P$). The plotted points therefore all lie on the vertical straight line $PV = 303\,nR\,\mathrm{J}$, parallel to the $P$-axis. The key idea is that $PV$ depends only on the temperature; a hyperbola would appear only on a $P$-versus-$V$ plot, not on a $P$-versus-$PV$ plot.
hint: At fixed temperature, what single value must the product $PV$ take?

question: For an ideal gas, three thermodynamic processes labelled 1, 2 and 3 are shown on a $PV$ diagram. All three start from the same initial state $(P_0,V_0)$ and end at the same larger final volume. In the figure, curve 1 is a horizontal line at constant pressure $P_0$; curve 2 is a hyperbola with $P\propto1/V$; curve 3 is the steepest curve, $P\propto1/V^{\gamma}$, ending at the lowest final pressure. One process is adiabatic, one is isobaric and one is isothermal. Which of the following correctly identifies the three processes?
solution: All three curves start at $(P_0,V_0)$ and end at the same final volume. The horizontal line (curve 1) keeps the pressure constant, so it is the isobar. The hyperbola (curve 2) follows Boyle's law $PV=\text{const}$, so it is the isotherm. The steepest curve (curve 3) follows $PV^\gamma=\text{const}$ with $\gamma>1$, so it is the adiabat: an adiabatic expansion cools the gas the most and ends at the lowest pressure and temperature. Hence adiabatic = 3, isobaric = 1, isothermal = 2, which is row (d). On a $PV$ diagram the steepness ordering is always isobar < isotherm < adiabat.
hint: On a $PV$ diagram the adiabat is steepest, the isotherm is $P\propto1/V$, and the isobar is horizontal.

question: For an ideal gas, three thermodynamic processes labelled 1, 2 and 3 are shown on a $PV$ diagram. All three start from the same initial state $(P_0,V_0)$ and end at the same larger final volume. In the figure, curve 1 is a horizontal line at constant pressure $P_0$; curve 2 is a hyperbola with $P\propto1/V$; curve 3 is the steepest curve, $P\propto1/V^{\gamma}$, ending at the lowest final pressure. One process is adiabatic, one is isobaric and one is isothermal. Which of the following correctly identifies the three processes?
solution: Each curve starts at the same state and ends at the same final volume. Curve 1 is horizontal, so the pressure never changes: it is the isobar. Curve 2 satisfies $PV=\text{const}$ (Boyle's law at fixed temperature): it is the isotherm. Curve 3 is the steepest, obeying $PV^\gamma=\text{const}$ with $\gamma=C_p/C_v>1$: it is the adiabat, because an adiabatic expansion does work at the expense of internal energy, cooling the gas and ending at the lowest pressure. Therefore adiabatic = 3, isobaric = 1, isothermal = 2 — row (d).
hint: On a $PV$ diagram the steepness ordering is always isobar (horizontal) < isotherm < adiabat (steepest).

question: An ideal gas is initially at temperature $T$ and volume $V$. Its volume increases by $\Delta V$ when the temperature rises by $\Delta T$ while the pressure stays constant. Define $\delta = \frac{\Delta V}{V\,\Delta T}$. Find $\delta$ as a function of $T$, and state how a graph of $\delta$ versus $T$ behaves.
answer: $\delta = \frac{1}{T}$ — it decreases with $T$ like $1/T$ (a falling hyperbola-shaped curve).
solution: Concept: an isobaric process of an ideal gas. Apply the ideal-gas law $pV = nRT$ to the small change at fixed $p$: $p\,\Delta V = nR\,\Delta T$, so $\frac{\Delta V}{V\,\Delta T} = \frac{nR}{pV}$. Using $pV = nRT$ once more gives $\delta = \frac{nR}{nRT} = \frac{1}{T}$. So $\delta$ is not constant: it falls inversely with the absolute temperature, and a plot of $\delta$ against $T$ is a decreasing hyperbola — doubling the absolute temperature halves $\delta$. Limit check: as $T \to \infty$, $\delta \to 0$, and the units $1/\mathrm{K}$ match the definition $\Delta V/(V\Delta T)$.
hint: Apply the ideal-gas law to the small isobaric expansion and eliminate the pressure.

question: In a room whose air is at 16 degree Celsius, three rulers — one of steel, one of wood, one of rubber — have been lying for hours. Which ruler is the coldest?

choices.label: D
choices.text: They will all be at the same temperature

solution: Concept: the zeroth law of thermodynamics — objects left in contact with their surroundings reach thermal equilibrium. After hours in the room, each ruler has exchanged heat with the air until no net heat flow remains, so every ruler sits at exactly the air temperature, 16 degrees Celsius; none is colder than another. Steel only FEELS coldest: its thermal conductivity is far larger than that of wood or rubber, so it drains heat from your 37 degree hand quickly and produces a stronger cold sensation. The sensation of cold reports the rate of heat flow out of your skin, not the object's temperature — choice D.
hint: Separate temperature (a state) from the feeling of cold (a rate of heat flow into your hand).

question: One mole of an ideal gas is taken along the process $A \to B \to C$ shown on a $pV$ diagram; points $A$ and $C$ lie on the same isotherm. What is the change in the internal energy of the gas along $A \to B \to C$?
solution: Concept: for a fixed amount of ideal gas the internal energy depends only on the temperature, $U = n C_V T$, and is a state function — its change depends only on the endpoints, never on the path. Since $A$ and $C$ lie on the SAME isotherm, $T_A = T_C$, so $\Delta U = n C_V (T_C - T_A) = 0$, whatever detour the path makes through $B$ — choice D. The listed expressions are of the work/heat type (areas under process curves), which need not vanish on a path that returns to the initial temperature; only $\Delta U$ is pinned to the temperature difference alone.
hint: Internal energy of an ideal gas is a state function of temperature alone — compare only the endpoints.

question: A hollow cylinder contains a monatomic ideal gas and is closed at the top by a movable piston. The only forces on the piston are the atmospheric pressure, the gas pressure and the piston's weight, so the gas pressure stays constant at $P_0$. If heat $Q$ is supplied slowly to the gas (heat capacities of cylinder and piston negligible), what is the change in volume of the gas?
solution: Because the piston is free and moves slowly, the gas pressure remains $P_0$: the process is isobaric. First law: $Q = \Delta U + W$. For a monatomic ideal gas $\Delta U = \frac{3}{2}nR\,\Delta T$, and the expansion work is $W = P_0\,\Delta V = nR\,\Delta T$ (ideal-gas law at fixed $P_0$). Hence $Q = \frac{5}{2}nR\,\Delta T = \frac{5}{2}P_0\,\Delta V$, i.e. $Q = nC_P\Delta T$ with the monatomic $C_P = \frac{5}{2}R$. Solving, $\Delta V = \frac{2Q}{5P_0}$ — option (a). Sanity check: only $2/5$ of the heat goes into internal energy while $3/5$ leaves as work, so $\Delta V$ must be smaller than $Q/P_0$, which it is.
hint: The free piston fixes the pressure, so use $Q = nC_P\Delta T$ with the monatomic $C_P$ and convert $\Delta T$ to $\Delta V$ via the ideal-gas law.

question: Assume that air is an ideal gas with molar mass $M$, and that the temperature $T$ of the atmosphere is independent of height. The atmospheric pressure at height $z$ above sea level is then given by the isothermal barometric law $p = p_0\, e^{-\lambda z}$ (the formula image was lost in the source OCR; this is its standard form). Find $\lambda$ in terms of $M$, $g$, $R$ and $T$.
solution: Concepts used: hydrostatic equilibrium plus the ideal-gas law. A thin layer of air at height $z$ supports the weight of the air above it: $dp = -\rho g\,dz$. For an ideal gas of molar mass $M$, the density is $\rho = pM/(RT)$. Substituting gives $\dfrac{dp}{p} = -\dfrac{Mg}{RT}\,dz$. Since $T$ is independent of height, integrate directly from $p_0$ at $z=0$: $\ln(p/p_0) = -Mgz/(RT)$, i.e. $p = p_0\,e^{-(Mg/RT)z}$. Comparing with $p = p_0 e^{-\lambda z}$ yields $\lambda = Mg/(RT)$. Unit check: $\mathrm{(kg/mol)(m/s^2) / (J/mol)} = \mathrm{m^{-1}}$ — an inverse length, as an exponent needs. Order-of-magnitude check: for air ($M = 0.029$ kg/mol, $T \approx 290$ K) $\lambda \approx 1.2\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$, i.e. the pressure falls by a factor $1/e$ every $\approx 8.5$ km — the well-known scale height of the atmosphere.
hint: Start from the hydrostatic relation $dp = -\rho g\,dz$ and write the gas density in terms of $p$, $M$ and $T$.

question: A 10 L container holds 10 moles of an ideal gas at an unknown initial temperature. You conduct a thermodynamic process in which, every second, the temperature drops by 2 K, the volume drops by 0.5 L, and the pressure drops by 9500 Pa, the gas remaining ideal throughout. What is the initial pressure of the gas? (The printed paper asks for the pressure 'after 2 s', but its options and marked key correspond to the initial pressure — see the solution.)
solution: Concept used: apply $pV = nRT$ to the initial state and to the state 2 s later, using the total changes over two seconds: $\Delta T = -4$ K, $\Delta V = -1.0$ L, $\Delta p = -19{,}000$ Pa, with $nR = 10 \times 8.314 = 83.14$ J/K. Initial state: $p_0 \times 0.010 = 83.14\,T_0$. State after 2 s: $(p_0 - 19000)\times 0.009 = 83.14\,(T_0 - 4)$. Substituting $T_0 = 0.010\,p_0/83.14$ into the second equation: $0.009\,p_0 - 171 = 0.010\,p_0 - 332.56$, so $0.001\,p_0 = 161.56$ and $p_0 = 161{,}560\ \mathrm{Pa} \approx 161.6$ kPa — option C. (The implied initial temperature is only $T_0 \approx 19.4$ K; the gas is treated as purely ideal.) Note on the wording: the pressure after 2 s would be $p_2 = p_0 - 19000 \approx 142.6$ kPa, which matches none of the four options, while $p_0 = 161.6$ kPa matches option C exactly — the paper's key clearly corresponds to the initial pressure computed here.
hint: Write $pV = nRT$ for the initial state and for the state 2 seconds later, then eliminate the unknown initial temperature between the two equations.

question: A hot-air balloon uses a gas flame to heat the air it contains so that it can hover a small distance above the ground. The combined mass of balloon, ropes, basket and riders is $M = 240\ \mathrm{kg}$ and the balloon's volume is $V = 1100\ \mathrm{m^3}$. The surrounding air is at $T_1 = 15^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($288\ \mathrm{K}$) with density $\rho_1 = 1.23\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$. Assuming the air inside is at the same (atmospheric) pressure as outside, to what temperature must the air in the balloon be heated?
solution: Hovering requires the buoyant force to equal the total weight: $\rho_1 V g = (M + \rho_2 V)g$, where $\rho_2$ is the required density of the hot air inside (the lifted load is the envelope plus the enclosed air). Solve for $\rho_2$: $\rho_2 = \rho_1 - \frac{M}{V} = 1.23 - \frac{240}{1100} = 1.0118\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$. Because the inside and outside pressures are equal, the ideal gas law in the form $\rho = \frac{p\,M_{\rm mol}}{R\,T}$ gives $\rho T = \text{constant}$ (density inversely proportional to absolute temperature at fixed pressure). Hence $T_2 = T_1\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2} = 288 \times \frac{1.23}{1.0118} = 350\ \mathrm{K} \approx 77^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Sanity check: the balloon must expel a mass fraction $0.218/1.23 \approx 18\%$ of its air, so the absolute temperature must rise by about $\frac{1}{0.82} - 1 \approx 22\%$: $288\ \mathrm{K} \to \sim\!350\ \mathrm{K}$ — consistent.
hint: First find the density the inside air must have for buoyancy to balance the total weight, then use the ideal-gas relation between density and absolute temperature at constant pressure.

question: A small house is kept warm by an electric heater of power $P = 1\ \mathrm{kW}$, which maintains the interior temperature at $t_1 = 19\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ while the outside temperature is $t_0 = 0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. A man enters the house, whereupon the room temperature rises and settles at a new value $t_2 = 20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assuming the house loses heat to the outside at a rate proportional to the inside-outside temperature difference, find the "heating power" of the man.
solution: Concept: Newton's law of cooling — the heat loss rate of the house is $K\,(t_{\mathrm{in}} - t_0)$, where $K$ is a constant loss coefficient in W per degree; at steady state the heat input equals the heat loss. Before the man enters: $P = K(t_1 - t_0)$, so $1000 = K \times 19$, giving $K = 1000/19 \approx 52.6\ \mathrm{W/^\circ C}$. After the man joins, the new steady state satisfies $1000 + P_{\mathrm{man}} = K(t_2 - t_0) = K \times 20$. Hence $P_{\mathrm{man}} = 20K - 1000 = \dfrac{20000}{19} - 1000 = \dfrac{1000}{19} \approx 52.6\ \mathrm{W}$. Sanity check: raising the equilibrium temperature by $1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ requires exactly one extra 'step' $K \times 1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} \approx 53\ \mathrm{W}$ of heating, which is precisely what the man supplies — a human body (~100 W metabolic, partly used) delivering ~50 W of effective room heating is physically reasonable.
hint: At steady state, heat in equals heat out, and the heat loss grows in proportion to the temperature difference with the outside.

question: A certain amount of water is heated from $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ using an $800\,\mathrm{W}$ immersion heater. We expect to heat the water in $210\,\mathrm{s}$, but instead it takes $230\,\mathrm{s}$. Determine the heat capacity of the vessel. (Ignore other heat losses.)
solution: In the expected $210\,\mathrm{s}$ the heater would supply exactly the energy the water needs: $E_{water} = 800\times210 = 1.68\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$. The observed time is $230\,\mathrm{s}$, so the extra energy $800\times(230-210) = 1.6\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{J}$ was absorbed by the vessel, which warmed through the same temperature rise $\Delta T = 40 - 20 = 20\,\mathrm{K}$ (it is in thermal contact with the water the whole time). Heat capacity $C = E/\Delta T = 1.6\times10^{4}/20 = 800\,\mathrm{J/K}$. Sanity check: the units are correct, and an $800\,\mathrm{J/K}$ vessel (comparable to about $0.8\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water) soaking up $16\,\mathrm{kJ}$ over $20\,\mathrm{K}$ is a reasonable value for the container of a heating experiment.
hint: The extra heating time beyond $210\,\mathrm{s}$ corresponds to the energy soaked up by the vessel while it warms through the same $20\,\mathrm{K}$.

question: A perfectly spherical elastic balloon of diameter $0.2\ \mathrm{m}$ is filled with hydrogen gas at sea level, then rises to an altitude where the atmospheric pressure is $0.65\ \mathrm{atm}$. The temperature stays the same. What is the balloon's diameter at that altitude?
solution: An elastic balloon with negligible wall tension always has the same pressure inside as outside, so the gas expands isothermally as the external pressure falls. Boyle's law: $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = V_1(P_1/P_2) = V_1/0.65 = 1.538\,V_1$. For a sphere $V \propto d^3$, so the diameter grows only as the cube root of the volume ratio: $d_2 = d_1(1/0.65)^{1/3} = 0.2 \times 1.154\ \mathrm{m} \approx 0.23\ \mathrm{m}$ (choice B). Sanity check: a 35% pressure drop raises the volume by about 54% but the diameter by only about 15% — cube roots grow slowly, so answers like $0.32\ \mathrm{m}$ (which would need roughly triple the volume) are far too large.
hint: At fixed temperature $PV$ is constant, but the diameter scales as the cube root of the volume ratio.

question: Different amounts of water at different temperatures are mixed: 1 litre at $10^\circ$C, 2 litres at $20^\circ$C, 3 litres at $30^\circ$C, 4 litres at $40^\circ$C, 5 litres at $50^\circ$C, 6 litres at $60^\circ$C, 7 litres at $70^\circ$C, 8 litres at $80^\circ$C and 9 litres at $90^\circ$C. What is the common temperature of the mixture if heat losses to the surroundings are negligible?
solution: Use conservation of energy: the heat released by the warm samples equals the heat absorbed by the cool ones. Since every sample is water, $Q_i = m_i c\,T_i$ with $m_i \propto V_i$ (same density) and the same specific heat $c$, so the final temperature is the volume-weighted mean: $T_f = \frac{\sum_i V_i T_i}{\sum_i V_i} = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^{9} n\cdot(10n)\,^\circ\mathrm{C}}{\sum_{n=1}^{9} n}$. Here $\sum_{n=1}^{9} n^2 = \frac{9\cdot10\cdot19}{6} = 285$ and $\sum n = 45$, giving $T_f = \frac{10\times 285}{45} = 63.3^\circ$C, i.e. option D. The plain average $50^\circ$C (option C) would be correct only if all volumes were equal; here the larger volumes are the warmer ones, so they dominate and pull the final temperature above the average. Sanity check: the result must lie between $10^\circ$C and $90^\circ$C and closer to the warm side, which $63^\circ$C is.
hint: Weight each temperature by the amount of water carrying it, not by the number of samples - think $Q = mc\Delta T$ per litre.

question: A heating element is built into a boiler containing 10 L of water. Its power is so small that it cannot bring the water to its boiling point. After the water has been heated as long as possible (steady state reached), the heating is switched off, and during the first minute afterwards the water temperature falls by $1^\circ$C. What is the power rating of the heating element if the water equivalent of the boiler is 3 kg? (Take $c_{water} = 4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$.)
solution: In the steady state the water temperature no longer rises, so every joule supplied per second by the element is lost to the surroundings: $P = \dot{Q}_{loss}$. When heating stops, the water is at the same temperature, so heat initially keeps leaking at the same rate $P$; the observed fall of $1^\circ$C in the first minute therefore measures that leak rate: $P = (m_{water} + m_{eq})\,c\,\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}$. Here $m_{water} = 10$ kg (10 L of water), the water equivalent is $m_{eq} = 3$ kg, and $\Delta T/\Delta t = 1/60$ K/s. So $P = 13 \times 4200 \times \frac{1}{60} \approx 9.1\times10^2$ W $\approx 900$ W (using $c = 4186$ gives 907 W). Concept used: energy balance (first law) — the steady-state input power equals the heat-loss rate, which the cooling just after switch-off reveals. Answer A.
hint: At steady state the element's power exactly equals the rate of heat leakage — and the cooling in the first minute after switch-off tells you that leakage rate.

question: Two different quantities of the same fluid are mixed in the laboratory. The mass $m_1$ of the hotter sample is twice the mass $m_2$ of the cooler one, and the initial temperature $T_1$ of the hotter sample is twice the initial temperature $T_2 = 30^\circ\mathrm{C}$ of the other. Find the equilibrium temperature (no heat exchange with the surroundings).
solution: Calorimetry — energy conservation: heat lost by the hot sample equals heat gained by the cold one. Both samples are the same fluid, so the specific heat $c$ is common and cancels: $m_1 c(T_1 - T) = m_2 c(T - T_2)$. With $m_1 = 2m_2$ and $T_1 = 2T_2 = 60^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $2m_2(60 - T) = m_2(T - 30)$, so $120 - 2T = T - 30$, giving $3T = 150$ and $T = 50^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Sanity check: the result lies between 30 °C and 60 °C and is pulled toward the hot temperature because the hot sample has twice the mass. Answer (C).
hint: Write 'heat lost by the hot sample = heat gained by the cold one'; the common specific heat cancels.

question: An ideal gas expands adiabatically so that its volume doubles from $V_0$ to $2V_0$. Taking $\gamma = 5/3$ (monatomic gas), what happens to the initial temperature $T_0$?
solution: For a reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas, $TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{const}$. Hence $T = T_0\left(V_0/2V_0\right)^{\gamma-1} = T_0\,2^{-(\gamma-1)}$. With $\gamma = 5/3$: $T = T_0\,2^{-2/3} = T_0/2^{2/3} = T_0/1.59 \approx 0.63\,T_0$. Physically the gas cools because it does work on the surroundings with no heat input (first law with $Q = 0$: $W = -\Delta U$). Option (A) quotes the reciprocal factor 1.59 but calls it a rise — an adiabatic expansion must always cool the gas. Answer (E).
hint: Use the adiabatic temperature–volume relation; note that $2^{2/3} \approx 1.59$.

question: A Carnot cycle is run in reverse as a refrigeration cycle (counterclockwise on the $PV$ diagram) between a hot reservoir at $T_H$ and a cold reservoir at $T_C$. If the efficiency is computed as for an engine, $e=\frac{\text{net work done by the gas}}{\text{heat absorbed by the gas}}$, the result is …
solution: Run in reverse, the working substance absorbs $Q_C$ isothermally at $T_C$ (refrigeration — heat is taken from the cold side) and rejects $Q_H$ at $T_H$, with the Carnot ratio $Q_H/Q_C=T_H/T_C$. The net work done BY the gas over the cycle is $W=Q_C-Q_H<0$: work is put IN, not extracted. Feeding this into the engine definition, $e=W/Q_{\text{absorbed}}=\frac{Q_C-Q_H}{Q_C}=1-\frac{Q_H}{Q_C}=1-\frac{T_H}{T_C}$, which is negative because $T_H>T_C$. The negative value is the physics: a refrigerator consumes work rather than producing it, so engine efficiency is not the right figure of merit — the coefficient of performance $Q_C/W_{\text{in}}$ is used instead. Option A is the efficiency of the same cycle run forward as an engine.
hint: In reverse, which reservoir supplies heat to the gas — and what sign does the net work done by the gas have?

question: An ideal monatomic gas expands quasi-statically to twice its initial volume. If the process is isothermal, the work done by the gas is $W_i$; if the process is adiabatic, the work done by the gas is $W_a$. Which of the following is true?
solution: In both processes the gas expands, so $\int P\,dV > 0$: both works are positive, eliminating options (B) and (D). On a $P$-$V$ diagram drawn from the same initial state, the isotherm ($P \propto 1/V$) lies above the adiabat ($P \propto V^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma = 5/3 > 1$ for a monatomic gas), because the expanding adiabatic gas does work at the expense of its internal energy and cools, while the isothermal gas keeps its temperature by absorbing heat. The work is the area under the curve up to $2V$, so $W_i > W_a > 0$. Numerically: $W_i = nRT\ln 2 \approx 0.693\,nRT$, while $W_a = nC_V(T_i - T_f) = \frac{3}{2}nRT_i\left(1 - 2^{-2/3}\right) \approx 0.555\,nRT_i$, confirming $0 < W_a < W_i$.
hint: Sketch the isotherm and the adiabat through the same initial point on a $P$-$V$ diagram: which curve stays higher as $V$ doubles?

question: A gaseous mixture of $O_2$ (molecular mass 32 u) and $N_2$ (molecular mass 28 u) is maintained at constant temperature. What is the ratio $\frac{v_{\text{rms}}(O_2)}{v_{\text{rms}}(N_2)}$ of the root-mean-square speeds of the two kinds of molecules?
solution: From kinetic theory, $\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$, so the rms speed of an ideal-gas molecule is $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3k_BT/m}$, set by the temperature and the molecular mass alone. At the same temperature, $\frac{v_{\text{rms}}(O_2)}{v_{\text{rms}}(N_2)} = \sqrt{\frac{m_{N_2}}{m_{O_2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{28\,\text{u}}{32\,\text{u}}} = \sqrt{\frac{7}{8}} \approx 0.94$. The ratio must be less than 1 because the heavier $O_2$ molecules move more slowly on average than the lighter $N_2$ molecules at the same temperature — this immediately rules out option (C), which exceeds 1, and option (A), which forgets the square root that the $v \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$ relation requires.
hint: At equal temperature the rms speed depends only on molecular mass — and keep track of where the square root sits.

question: In an adiabatic process involving an ideal gas, the gas expands and does $500\ \mathrm{J}$ of work on its surroundings. What is the change in the internal energy $\Delta U$ of the gas?
solution: Use the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta U = Q - W_{\text{by}}$, where $W_{\text{by}}$ is the work done by the gas on its surroundings. The process is adiabatic, so no heat enters or leaves: $Q = 0$. The gas expands and does $+500\ \mathrm{J}$ of work on the surroundings, so $\Delta U = 0 - 500\ \mathrm{J} = -500\ \mathrm{J}$. Physically, the gas spends internal energy to push the surroundings out with no heat input, so its internal energy (and temperature) must drop — exactly the cooling seen in adiabatic expansion. Quick check: if the gas were compressed adiabatically instead, the sign of the work would reverse and $\Delta U$ would be positive, consistent with heating by compression.
hint: Apply the first law with $Q=0$; be careful about the sign of the work done by the gas.

question: The root-mean-square (RMS) speed of oxygen molecules ($O_2$) is $v$ at a certain temperature $T$. If the gas is heated so that its absolute temperature is quadrupled and the diatomic oxygen molecules dissociate into individual oxygen atoms, what will be the RMS speed of the resulting atomic gas?
solution: The RMS speed comes from $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3k_B T/m}$. Two changes happen at once: the temperature quadruples ($T \to 4T$) and each $O_2$ molecule of mass $m$ splits into two oxygen atoms of mass $m/2$. Therefore $v_{rms}' = \sqrt{3k_B(4T)/(m/2)} = \sqrt{8 \cdot 3k_BT/m} = \sqrt{8}\,v = 2\sqrt2\,v$. Physically, hotter and lighter particles both move faster, so the new speed must exceed $v$ — ruling out $v/2$ and $v/\sqrt2$. Answer (E).
hint: RMS speed goes as the square root of temperature divided by particle mass — apply both changes inside the square root.

question: An ideal gas undergoes a process $P = kV^2$. Starting from the state $(P_0, V_0)$, what is the work done by the gas when its volume becomes $2V_0$?
solution: Work in a quasistatic process is the area under the $P$–$V$ curve: $W = \int_{V_0}^{2V_0} P\,dV$. First fix $k$ from the initial state: $P_0 = kV_0^2 \Rightarrow k = P_0/V_0^2$. Then $W = \int_{V_0}^{2V_0} kV^2\,dV = \dfrac{k}{3}\left[(2V_0)^3 - V_0^3\right] = \dfrac{7kV_0^3}{3} = \dfrac{7}{3}P_0V_0$. Sanity check: during the expansion the pressure climbs from $P_0$ to $4P_0$, so the work must exceed $P_0V_0$ (the value if $P$ stayed at $P_0$) and stay below $4P_0V_0$ (the value if $P$ jumped to $4P_0$ at once); $7/3 \approx 2.33$ sits nicely in between. Answer (D).
hint: Work is the integral of $P\,dV$; express the constant $k$ from the initial state before integrating.

question: The initial pressure and volume of one mole of an ideal gas are $10^5$ Pa and 6 L respectively. The gas is compressed adiabatically to a volume of 2 L. What is the approximate amount of work done on the gas? (Assume $C_V = 3R/2$.)
solution: With $C_V = 3R/2$ the gas is monatomic, $\gamma = C_P/C_V = 5/3$. Initial temperature from the ideal gas law: $T_1 = P_1V_1/(nR) = (10^5 \times 6\times 10^{-3})/(8.314) \approx 72$ K. For the adiabatic process $TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{const}$, so $T_2 = T_1 (V_1/V_2)^{\gamma-1} = 72 \times 3^{2/3} \approx 150$ K. Since $Q = 0$ adiabatically, the first law gives the work done on the gas as the internal-energy increase: $W_{\text{on}} = nC_V(T_2 - T_1) = \frac{3}{2} \times 8.314 \times (150 - 72) \approx 972$ J (option D). Cross-check via $W = (P_2V_2 - P_1V_1)/(\gamma - 1)$ with $P_2 = P_1(V_1/V_2)^{\gamma} \approx 4.33\times 10^5$ Pa gives the same $\approx 970$ J.
hint: Use $TV^{\gamma-1} = $ const with $\gamma = 5/3$ to get $T_2$, then $W = nC_V\Delta T$ because $Q = 0$.

question: A sample of helium gas occupying 5.6 L at STP is compressed adiabatically from 5.6 L to 0.7 L. What is the magnitude of the work done on the gas if the initial temperature is $T$ K? (Helium is monatomic, $\gamma = 5/3$.)
solution: At STP one mole occupies 22.4 L, so this sample contains $n = 5.6/22.4 = 0.25$ mol. The volume ratio is $V_1/V_2 = 5.6/0.7 = 8$. For the monatomic adiabatic compression, $T_2 = T_1(V_1/V_2)^{\gamma-1} = T\times 8^{2/3} = 4T$. Since $Q = 0$, the work done on the gas equals its internal-energy increase: $W = nC_V\Delta T = 0.25 \times \frac{3}{2}R\times(4T - T) = \frac{9}{8}RT$ (option C). The trick of the problem is the mole count hidden in the STP volume; using $W = nR(T_2 - T_1)/(\gamma-1) = \frac{0.25\,R\times 3T}{2/3}$ reproduces $\frac{9}{8}RT$.
hint: First convert 5.6 L at STP into moles, then find $T_2 = T(V_1/V_2)^{\gamma-1}$ and use $nC_V\Delta T$.

question: Two similar pots are filled with water at the same temperature $T$. One pot is then heated, and the other is cooled. In both cases, water overflows from the pots. What was the initial temperature of the water?
solution: Overflow in both directions is the decisive clue. On heating, water overflows if its density decreases with rising temperature; on cooling, it overflows if its density also decreases as the temperature falls. Both happening at once means the initial temperature sits exactly at the temperature of maximum density of water: heating above it and cooling below it both lower the density, so the volume grows and the pots overflow either way. Water is densest at $4\ ^\circ\text{C}$ owing to its anomalous expansion — below $4\ ^\circ\text{C}$, hydrogen-bonded, ice-like open clusters begin to form and the volume increases despite cooling. In kelvin: $T=273.15+4=277.15$ K — choice (B). This anomaly is why lakes freeze from the top while the bottom water stays near $4\ ^\circ\text{C}$, allowing fish to survive the winter.
hint: Think about the one special temperature at which water is densest.

question: For an ideal gas undergoing an adiabatic process, its pressure $P$ and absolute temperature $T$ are related by $P\propto T^{n}$. If $C_p/C_v=3/2$, what is the value of $n$?
solution: For one mole of ideal gas $PV=RT$, and a reversible adiabatic change obeys $PV^{\gamma}=\mathrm{const}$ with $\gamma=C_p/C_v=3/2$. Substitute $V=RT/P$ into the adiabatic law: $P\,(RT/P)^{\gamma}=\mathrm{const}$, i.e. $P^{1-\gamma}T^{\gamma}=\mathrm{const}$, which rearranges to $P\propto T^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}$. Hence $n=\dfrac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}=\dfrac{3/2}{1/2}=3$. Sanity check: for a monatomic gas ($\gamma=5/3$) the same formula gives $n=5/2$, the familiar adiabatic exponent relating $P$ and $T$; and as $\gamma\to1$ (isothermal limit) $n\to\infty$, consistent with $P$ and $T$ becoming independent along an isotherm. Note options (D) and (E) in the paper both read 3; the first correct choice is (D).
hint: Eliminate $V$ between $PV^{\gamma}=\mathrm{const}$ and $PV=RT$ to find how $P$ scales with $T$.

question: Three objects made of the same material, of masses $m$, $m$ and $3m$, are initially at temperatures $40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ respectively. They are brought into thermal contact with no heat loss to the surroundings. What will be their final common equilibrium temperature?
solution: All three objects share the same specific heat $c$ (same material). Conservation of energy — heat lost by the hot object equals heat gained by the cooler ones — gives $mc(40-T_f)+mc(50-T_f)+3mc(60-T_f)=0$, which is simply a mass-weighted average of the initial temperatures: $T_f=\dfrac{m\cdot40+m\cdot50+3m\cdot60}{m+m+3m}=\dfrac{40+50+180}{5}=54^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Check: the first body warms by $14^{\circ}$ and the second by $4^{\circ}$ (total gain $18mc$), while the $3m$ body cools by $6^{\circ}$ (loss $18mc$) — the energy books balance, confirming option (D).
hint: With equal specific heats, energy conservation makes the final temperature the mass-weighted mean of the initial temperatures.

question: The root-mean-square (RMS) speed of an oxygen molecule ($\mathrm{O_2}$) is $v$ at a particular temperature. If the absolute temperature is doubled and the molecules dissociate into oxygen atoms, what will be their RMS speed?
solution: The RMS speed of gas particles follows from $\tfrac{1}{2}m\,v_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}=\tfrac{3}{2}kT$, i.e. $v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{3kT/m}$. An $\mathrm{O_2}$ molecule has mass $32u$; after dissociation each O atom has $m'=16u=\tfrac{m}{2}$. With the temperature doubled, $T'=2T$: $v'=\sqrt{\dfrac{3k(2T)}{m/2}}=\sqrt{4\cdot\dfrac{3kT}{m}}=2v$. The two changes multiply: doubling $T$ alone would give $\sqrt{2}\,v$, and halving the particle mass another factor $\sqrt{2}$, together a factor of 2 — option (A).
hint: $v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{3kT/m}$: track how both $T$ and the particle mass change.

question: The internal energy of a gas undergoing an adiabatic process is given by $U = a + bPV$, where $a$ and $b$ are nonzero constants. What is the ratio $γ = C_P/C_V$ of the molar heat capacities of the gas?
solution: For one mole of ideal gas $PV = RT$, so $U = a + bPV = a + bRT$. The molar heat capacity at constant volume is $C_V = dU/dT = bR$, and for an ideal gas $C_P − C_V = R$, so $C_P = (b+1)R$. Hence $γ = C_P/C_V = (b+1)/b = 1 + 1/b$. Cross-check from the adiabatic condition itself: $dU = −P dV$ gives $b(P dV + V dP) = −P dV$, i.e. $dP/P = −((1+b)/b)·dV/V$, so $PV^{(1+b)/b} = const$, identifying $γ = 1 + 1/b$ again. Both routes agree on choice E.
hint: Express U in terms of T using PV = RT for one mole, then use C_P − C_V = R for an ideal gas.

question: The previous part found that atoms in the anharmonic potential $\frac{1}{2}kx^2 - gx^3$ have a mean displacement $\langle x\rangle = 3gk_BT/k^2$ that grows linearly with temperature. What is the physical significance of this result?
answer: It is the microscopic origin of thermal expansion: the mean interatomic separation grows linearly with $T$, whereas a purely harmonic (symmetric) potential would give zero expansion.
solution: In a purely harmonic solid ($V \propto x^2$, symmetric) parts (a) and (b) give $\langle x\rangle = 0$ at every temperature: heating only increases the vibration amplitude $\sqrt{\langle x^2\rangle} \propto \sqrt{T}$ but never shifts the mean position, so the solid would not expand at all. The small asymmetric term $-gx^3$ changes that: the wall is stiffer for $x < 0$ and softer for $x > 0$, so more energetic (hotter) atoms spend more of their time displaced toward the soft side, giving $\langle x\rangle = 3gk_BT/k^2 \propto T$. Since the mean interatomic spacing fixes the macroscopic length of the sample, the whole solid expands linearly with temperature -- the familiar law $\Delta L = \alpha L\,\Delta T$. Thermal expansion is thus inherently an anharmonic effect.
hint: Compare with the harmonic case where the mean spacing never changes: a temperature-proportional mean spacing means the whole solid must grow as it warms.

question: A closed horizontal cylinder has adiabatic walls and is divided into three compartments $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$ by two frictionless pistons $S_1$ (adiabatic) and $S_2$ (conducting), free to move along the cylinder. Initially each compartment holds 1 mole of helium (ideal monatomic gas: $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$, $C_p = \frac{5}{2}R$, $\gamma = \frac{5}{3}$) at pressure $P_0$, volume $V_0$, temperature $T_0$. Heat is now supplied slowly to $A_1$ until the temperature of $A_3$ becomes $T_3 = \frac{9}{4}T_0$. Determine the final thermodynamic states $\{P_1, V_1, T_1\}$, $\{P_2, V_2, T_2\}$, $\{P_3, V_3, T_3\}$ of the three compartments, expressing pressures in terms of $P_0$, volumes in terms of $V_0$ and temperatures in terms of $T_0$.
solution: Concept: quasi-static frictionless pistons force mechanical equilibrium ($P_1 = P_2 = P_3 \equiv P$) and the conducting $S_2$ forces $T_2 = T_3$; with one mole in each of $A_2$ and $A_3$, the ideal-gas law then gives $V_2 = V_3$. Treat $A_2 \cup A_3$ (2 moles) as one system: its boundary (adiabatic $S_1$ and adiabatic walls) passes no heat, so it is compressed reversibly adiabatically: $P(2V_2)^{\gamma} = P_0(2V_0)^{\gamma}$, i.e. $P V_2^{\gamma} = P_0 V_0^{\gamma}$. One mole in $A_3$ obeys $P V_2 = R T_3 = \frac{9}{4}P_0 V_0$. Dividing the two relations: $V_2^{\gamma-1} = \frac{4}{9}V_0^{\gamma-1}$, so $V_2 = \left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^{1/(\gamma-1)}V_0 = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{3}V_0 = \frac{8}{27}V_0$. Then $P = \frac{(9/4)P_0 V_0}{V_2} = \frac{243}{32}P_0$; total-volume conservation gives $V_1 = 3V_0 - 2V_2 = \frac{65}{27}V_0$; finally $T_1 = \frac{P V_1}{R} = \frac{243}{32}\cdot\frac{65}{27}T_0 = \frac{585}{32}T_0 \approx 18.3\,T_0$. Sanity check: the adiabatically compressed $A_2, A_3$ warm up ($T_3 > T_0$) while shrinking ($V_2 < V_0$), as expected.
hint: Lump A2 and A3 into one adiabatically compressed system; T2 = T3 and P2 = P3 force V2 = V3.

question: Using the final states found previously — common final pressure $P = \frac{243}{32}P_0$, final temperatures $T_2 = T_3 = \frac{9}{4}T_0$ and volumes $V_2 = V_3 = \frac{8}{27}V_0$ — find the total work done by the gas in $A_1$ on the gases in $A_2$ and $A_3$, expressed in terms of $P_0 V_0$.
solution: Concept: first law applied to the combined system $A_2 \cup A_3$. That combined system receives no heat — piston $S_1$ is adiabatic and the cylinder walls are adiabatic, while $S_2$ is internal to the combined system — so the work done ON it equals its internal-energy gain: $W_{\mathrm{on}} = \Delta U = n C_V \Delta T$ with $n = 2$ moles and $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$. Hence $\Delta U = 2\cdot\frac{3}{2}R\left(\frac{9}{4}T_0 - T_0\right) = 3R\cdot\frac{5}{4}T_0 = \frac{15}{4}RT_0$. The piston $S_1$ transmits this work directly, so the gas in $A_1$ does $W = \frac{15}{4}P_0 V_0$ (using $P_0 V_0 = RT_0$) on $A_2$ and $A_3$. Magnitude check: at $T_0 = 300$ K, $W \approx 3.75\times8.31\times300 \approx 9.4$ kJ — plausible for adiabatically compressing 2 moles.
hint: The combined A2+A3 system is adiabatic, so the work it receives is exactly its internal-energy change.

question: Using the previous results — final temperature of $A_1$ equal to $T_1 = \frac{585}{32}T_0$ and work done by $A_1$ equal to $W = \frac{15}{4}P_0 V_0$ — find the amount of heat supplied to the gas in $A_1$, expressed in terms of $P_0 V_0$.
solution: Concept: first law for $A_1$ alone: $Q_1 = \Delta U_1 + W_{\mathrm{by}}$. Compartment $A_1$ holds 1 mole, so $\Delta U_1 = C_V (T_1 - T_0) = \frac{3}{2}R\left(\frac{585}{32} - 1\right)T_0 = \frac{3}{2}R\cdot\frac{553}{32}T_0 = \frac{1659}{64}RT_0$. The work done by $A_1$ is $\frac{15}{4}RT_0 = \frac{240}{64}RT_0$. Hence $Q_1 = \frac{1659 + 240}{64}RT_0 = \frac{1899}{64}RT_0 = \frac{1899}{64}P_0 V_0 \approx 29.7\,P_0 V_0$. Check: most of the heat goes into $A_1$'s own internal energy (its temperature rises by a factor of about 18), and only $\frac{15}{4}/29.7 \approx 13\%$ leaves as work on the other compartments — consistent with the large temperature rise of $A_1$.
hint: Apply the first law to A1: heat in equals its internal-energy rise (use T1 = 585/32 T0) plus work out.

question: A monoatomic ideal gas is kept at a temperature of $47\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. A dust particle of mass $0.0001\ \mathrm{g}$ is introduced into the gas and is knocked about by the gas molecules for a very long time (one year). What will its (root-mean-square) speed be? Explain how you should proceed to calculate this. (Take $k_{B}=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.)
solution: The key idea is equipartition of energy: in thermal equilibrium any particle suspended in a gas - however massive - acquires the same average translational kinetic energy as a gas molecule, $\frac{1}{2}m\langle v^{2}\rangle=\frac{3}{2}k_{B}T$ (each translational degree of freedom carries $\frac{1}{2}k_{B}T$). The molecular collisions bring the grain to this thermal speed in a tiny fraction of a second, far less than a year; thereafter its rms speed stays constant - it executes Brownian motion, but $\sqrt{\langle v^{2}\rangle}$ does not grow with time, so the answer is time-independent. With $T=47+273=320$ K and $m=0.0001\ \mathrm{g}=10^{-7}$ kg: $v_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{3\times1.38\times10^{-23}\times320}{10^{-7}}}=\sqrt{1.32\times10^{-13}}=3.6\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. This is far below the molecular speed ($\sim500\ \mathrm{m/s}$) because the grain is enormously heavier - equipartition equalizes energies, not speeds.
hint: Think of equipartition of energy: what average translational kinetic energy does any particle suspended in a gas at temperature $T$ eventually acquire, regardless of its mass?

question: A refrigerating machine of maximum theoretical efficiency (a reversible, Carnot refrigerator) transfers the heat released when one mole of water is cooled from $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($298\ \mathrm{K}$) to $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($273\ \mathrm{K}$) and then frozen at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$, into a second mole of water, heating it from $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($373\ \mathrm{K}$) and boiling part of it at $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$. How many moles of water are converted to steam at $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$? Data: molar heat capacity of liquid water $c = 75.3\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$; latent heat of fusion $L_f = 6.02\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$ at $273\ \mathrm{K}$; latent heat of boiling $L_v = 40.68\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$ at $373\ \mathrm{K}$.
solution: A maximally efficient refrigerator is reversible, so the entropy it removes from the cold water equals the entropy it delivers to the warm water (work carries no entropy). Entropy given up by the first mole: cooling, $c\ln(298/273) = 75.3\times0.0876 = 6.60\ \mathrm{J/K}$; freezing, $L_f/273 = 6020/273 = 22.05\ \mathrm{J/K}$; total $28.65\ \mathrm{J/K}$. Entropy taken up by the second mole: heating, $c\ln(373/298) = 75.3\times0.2245 = 16.90\ \mathrm{J/K}$; boiling $n$ moles at $373\ \mathrm{K}$, $nL_v/373 = 109.06n\ \mathrm{J/K}$. Reversibility demands $16.90 + 109.06n = 28.65$, so $n = 11.75/109.06 = 0.108\ \mathrm{mol}$. The second law does the real work here: a plain energy balance could not fix $n$, because it ignores the quality (temperature) of the transferred heat.
hint: A maximally efficient refrigerator is reversible, so the entropy given up by the cooling-and-freezing mole equals the entropy gained by the heating-and-boiling mole.

question: Continuing the previous problem: a reversible refrigerator pumps the heat released by one mole of water cooling from $298\ \mathrm{K}$ to $273\ \mathrm{K}$ and freezing there ($c = 75.3\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, $L_f = 6.02\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$) into a second mole, heating it from $298\ \mathrm{K}$ to $373\ \mathrm{K}$ and vaporizing $n = 0.108$ mol of it at $373\ \mathrm{K}$ ($L_v = 40.68\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$). How much work must be done by the refrigerator?
solution: Apply the first law to the refrigerator working in a cycle: $W = Q_h - Q_c$, where $Q_c$ is heat absorbed from the cold water and $Q_h$ is heat delivered to the warm water. Heat extracted: $Q_c = c(298-273) + L_f = 75.3\times25 + 6020 = 1883 + 6020 = 7.90\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$. Heat delivered: $Q_h = c(373-298) + nL_v = 75.3\times75 + 0.108\times40680 = 5648 + 4381 = 1.003\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$. Hence $W = 10028 - 7903 \approx 2.13\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J} \approx 2.1\ \mathrm{kJ}$. Sanity checks: $W > 0$ because heat is pumped from colder to hotter bodies, and $W$ is much smaller than $Q_c$ because the temperature lift is modest -- a reversible refrigerator has a large coefficient of performance here.
hint: Work equals the heat dumped into the warm mole minus the heat extracted from the cold one; add up both the warming and the phase-change contributions on each side.

question: Atoms in a solid move in the anharmonic potential $V(x) = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 - gx^3$. At temperature $T$ the Boltzmann probability density of the displacement is $P(x) \propto e^{-V(x)/k_BT}$. Treating $gx^3$ as a small perturbation and using the harmonic (symmetric) results $\langle x^2\rangle_0 = k_BT/k$ and $\langle x^4\rangle_0 = 3\langle x^2\rangle_0^2 = 3(k_BT/k)^2$, find the average equilibrium position $\langle x\rangle$ of the atoms as a function of temperature.
solution: With $\beta = 1/k_BT$, factorize the Boltzmann factor: $e^{-\beta V} = e^{-\beta kx^2/2}\,e^{+\beta gx^3} \approx (1 + \beta gx^3)\,e^{-\beta kx^2/2}$, keeping first order in $g$. The normalization integral is unchanged to this order (the $x^3$ term is odd and integrates to zero over symmetric limits). The mean displacement becomes $\langle x\rangle = \dfrac{\int x(1 + \beta gx^3)e^{-\beta kx^2/2}dx}{\int e^{-\beta kx^2/2}dx} = \beta g\,\langle x^4\rangle_0 = \beta g\cdot3\left(\dfrac{k_BT}{k}\right)^2 = \dfrac{3gk_BT}{k^2}$. The displacement is positive and grows linearly with $T$: hotter atoms wander farther into the soft ($+x$) side of the asymmetric well. Equivalently, solving $m\ddot{x} = -kx + 3gx^2$ perturbatively for oscillations of energy $E$ gives $\langle x\rangle_E = 3gE/k^2$, and averaging with $\langle E\rangle = k_BT$ from part (b) gives the same answer.
hint: Expand the Boltzmann factor to first order in the anharmonic term; the odd correction converts the vanishing average of x into a constant times the fourth moment of the Gaussian.

question: Model a patch of ground with heat capacity per unit area $c$ and emissivity $\varepsilon$, illuminated by light of intensity $I$, ignoring all heat transfer except radiation (no atmosphere, no conduction/convection, no exchange between surface areas). The patch has temperature $T$. Develop an equation relating $dT/dt$ to $I$, $T$, $c$, $\varepsilon$, and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$.
solution: Concept: energy balance (first law) for a surface, with Stefan-Boltzmann radiation loss. Per unit area, the patch absorbs energy at rate $I$ and radiates at rate $\varepsilon\sigma T^4$ — a graybody whose emissivity $\varepsilon$ scales the blackbody flux $\sigma T^4$. The net power per unit area changes the patch's stored thermal energy, which per unit area is $cT$ ($c$ is the heat capacity per unit area). Therefore $c\,dT/dt = I - \varepsilon\sigma T^4$. Units check: $c$ is J/(m$^2\cdot$K), so $c\,dT/dt$ is W/m$^2$, matching $I$ and $\sigma T^4$. Setting $dT/dt = 0$ gives the radiative equilibrium $I = \varepsilon\sigma T^4$, which fixes the mean temperature.
hint: Write a per-area power budget: intensity in, graybody Stefan-Boltzmann radiation out, and the difference heating the patch.

question:
Starting from the ground-patch energy balance $c\,dT/dt = I - \varepsilon\sigma T^4$, take the annually varying intensity $I = I_0 + I_1\sin(\omega t)$ and write the temperature as $T = T_0 + T_1\sin(\omega t - \phi)$ with $T_1 \ll T_0$. Show that the equation reduces to the form
$A + B\sin(\omega t - \phi) + C\cos(\omega t - \phi) = I_0 + I_1\sin(\omega t)$,
and provide expressions for $A$, $B$, and $C$ in terms of $T_1$, $T_0$, $c$, $\varepsilon$, $\sigma$, and $\omega$.
solution: Concept: linearize the Stefan-Boltzmann law for small oscillations (Taylor/binomial expansion). Since $T_1 \ll T_0$: $T^4 = (T_0 + T_1\sin)^4 \approx T_0^4 + 4T_0^3T_1\sin(\omega t-\phi)$, keeping only first-order terms. Also $dT/dt = \omega T_1\cos(\omega t-\phi)$. Substituting into the balance equation: $c\omega T_1\cos(\omega t-\phi) = I_0 + I_1\sin\omega t - \varepsilon\sigma T_0^4 - 4\varepsilon\sigma T_0^3T_1\sin(\omega t-\phi)$. Moving the $T$-dependent terms to the left yields exactly the stated form with $A = \varepsilon\sigma T_0^4$ (mean radiative emission), $B = 4\varepsilon\sigma T_0^3T_1$ (radiative restoring term, in phase with $T$), and $C = c\omega T_1$ (thermal-inertia term, in quadrature). The factor 4 is $d(T^4)/dT = 4T^3$ — radiative feedback.
hint: Taylor-expand $T^4$ about $T_0$ to first order in $T_1$ and differentiate the assumed sinusoidal temperature.

question: Equation (1) from the seasonal-model derivation reads $A + B\sin(\omega t - \phi) + C\cos(\omega t - \phi) = I_0 + I_1\sin(\omega t)$, where $A$, $B$, $C$ were previously expressed through $T_0$, $T_1$, $c$, $\varepsilon$, $\sigma$, $\omega$. Using equation (1) itself, find expressions for $A$, $B$, and $C$ in terms of $I_0$, $I_1$, and $\phi$ by matching the two sides.
solution: Concept: matching coefficients of linearly independent harmonics. Rewrite the forcing sinusoid in the phase used on the left: $I_1\sin\omega t = I_1\sin[(\omega t-\phi)+\phi] = I_1\cos\phi\,\sin(\omega t-\phi) + I_1\sin\phi\,\cos(\omega t-\phi)$, using the angle-addition identity. Equating the constant part and the $\sin(\omega t-\phi)$ and $\cos(\omega t-\phi)$ coefficients independently (legitimate because a constant and the two quadrature sinusoids are linearly independent over a period) gives $A = I_0$, $B = I_1\cos\phi$, $C = I_1\sin\phi$. Consistency: $B^2 + C^2 = I_1^2$, and $C/B = \tan\phi$ — the split of the forcing between in-phase and quadrature components fixes the phase lag.
hint: Expand $I_1\sin\omega t$ in terms of $\sin(\omega t-\phi)$ and $\cos(\omega t-\phi)$ with the angle-addition formula, then match coefficients.

question: In the seasonal-temperature model, matching coefficients gave $A = \varepsilon\sigma T_0^4$, $B = 4\varepsilon\sigma T_0^3T_1$, $C = c\omega T_1$ from the physics, and $A = I_0$, $B = I_1\cos\phi$, $C = I_1\sin\phi$ from the forcing. Combine these results to obtain a simple relationship between the relative intensity amplitude $I_1/I_0$, the relative temperature amplitude $T_1/T_0$, and the phase shift $\phi$.
solution: Concept: divide the two independent coefficient matchings to eliminate the material constants. Constant terms: $I_0 = \varepsilon\sigma T_0^4$. In-phase terms: $I_1\cos\phi = 4\varepsilon\sigma T_0^3T_1$. Dividing the second by the first cancels $\varepsilon\sigma$: $\frac{I_1\cos\phi}{I_0} = \frac{4\varepsilon\sigma T_0^3T_1}{\varepsilon\sigma T_0^4} = 4\,\frac{T_1}{T_0}$, i.e. $\frac{I_1}{I_0} = \frac{4(T_1/T_0)}{\cos\phi}$. Interpretation: with zero lag ($\phi \to 0$) the relative temperature swing is one quarter of the relative forcing swing — the factor 4 is the $T^4$ radiative feedback. Thermal inertia (any lag $\phi > 0$) further reduces the response by $\cos\phi$; the quadrature match $\sin\phi = c\omega T_1/I_1$ separately fixes how $c$ sets the lag.
hint: Divide the $\sin$-coefficient equation by the constant-term equation; $\varepsilon\sigma$ cancels.

question: A hollow vertical cylinder of cross-sectional area $A$ contains a solid cylindrical piston of length $\ell$ (a close sliding fit; in the original figure the gas sits below the piston and the atmosphere above it). A fixed amount of ideal gas with molar heat capacity at constant volume $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$ is trapped beneath the piston; the bottom face of the piston initially sits at height $y_0$ above the closed bottom of the cylinder. Both the trapped gas and the outside atmosphere are at temperature $T_0$ and pressure $p_0$, and a pin holds the piston at rest. The pin is removed; the piston falls under gravity, compressing the gas adiabatically (no heat enters or leaves), and is momentarily at rest when its bottom face has dropped to $y_1 = y_0/8$. Find the density $\rho$ of the piston, in terms of $p_0$, $\ell$, and $A$ ($g$ is known).
solution: Apply energy conservation to the drop from $y_0$ to $y_1$ (the piston is at rest at both ends, so $\Delta KE = 0$). The downward forces doing work are gravity $mg$ and the atmosphere $p_0A$ on the top face, over $\Delta y = 7y_0/8$; the trapped gas is adiabatic, so the work done on the gas equals its internal-energy gain and is minus the work the gas does on the piston. Hence $(mg + p_0A)\frac{7y_0}{8} = \Delta U$. With $\gamma = (C_V+R)/C_V = 5/3$, adiabatic compression gives $T_1 = T_0(V_0/V_1)^{\gamma-1} = T_0\,8^{2/3} = 4T_0$, so $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T = \frac{3}{2}nR\cdot 3T_0 = \frac{9}{2}p_0Ay_0$, using the ideal gas law $nRT_0 = p_0V_0 = p_0Ay_0$. Therefore $mg = \frac{36}{7}p_0A - p_0A = \frac{29}{7}p_0A$, and with $m = \rho A\ell$ the area cancels: $\rho = \frac{29p_0}{7g\ell}$.
hint: Between the two instants of rest, the work by gravity and the atmosphere equals the gas's internal-energy gain; find the adiabatic temperature ratio first.

question: Same piston: ideal gas ($C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$) initially at $T_0$, $p_0$ beneath a piston whose bottom face starts at height $y_0$ in a cylinder of area $A$; released from rest it first drops adiabatically to $y_1 = y_0/8$ and, after bouncing, finally comes to rest at height $y_f$ once the gas has returned to thermal equilibrium with the surroundings at $T_0$. Using the result of part (a), $mg = \frac{29}{7}p_0A$ (i.e. $\rho = \frac{29p_0}{7g\ell}$), find the numerical value of the ratio $y_f/y_0$.
solution: At the final rest height the gas is back at $T_0$ - an isothermal final state - and the piston is in mechanical equilibrium, so the gas pressure must support piston plus atmosphere: $p_fA = p_0A + mg = p_0A(1 + 29/7) = \frac{36}{7}p_0A$. Because the gas amount and temperature are the same as initially, the ideal gas law gives $p_fV_f = p_0V_0$, and since $V = A\,y$ is set by the piston's bottom face, $\frac{y_f}{y_0} = \frac{p_0}{p_f} = \frac{7}{36} \approx 0.194$. Sanity check: this lies above the adiabatic bottom $y_1 = 0.125\,y_0$, because the gas at $y_f$ is cooler ($T_0$ instead of $4T_0$) and exerts less pressure at the same compression.
hint: The final state is isothermal and mechanically balanced - what pressure must the gas have to hold the piston up?

question: A simple gun consists of a uniform cylinder of length $L_0$ and inside radius $r_c$, sealed at one end by a movable plunger and plugged at the other by a cylindrical cork bullet held in place by friction with the walls. The pressure outside is $P_0$; the bullet just starts to slide out when the pressure inside exceeds $P_{cr}$. Initially the ideal monatomic gas inside is at temperature $T_0$, pressure $P_0$, column length $L_0$. The gas is heated while the plunger is held fixed (constant volume). Find the minimum gas temperature needed to launch the bullet, in terms of $r_c$, $T_0$, $L_0$, $P_0$, $P_{cr}$.
solution: With the plunger fixed the gas volume $V=\pi r_c^2 L_0$ stays constant, so the ideal-gas law in the form $P/T=\mathrm{const}$ (isochoric process) applies: $P/T=P_0/T_0$. The bullet breaks free exactly when the pressure reaches $P_{cr}$, so setting $P=P_{cr}$ gives $T_{\min}=T_0\,P_{cr}/P_0$. Since $P_{cr}>P_0$, the required temperature exceeds $T_0$, as expected. The radius $r_c$ and length $L_0$ cancel: at fixed volume the pressure depends only on temperature, so the geometry is irrelevant here.
hint: Which gas law applies when the volume is held fixed? Set the final pressure equal to the critical pressure and solve for $T$.

question: Same gun: cylinder of inside radius $r_c$, gas initially at temperature $T_0$, pressure $P_0$, column length $L_0$ (ideal monatomic gas, $\gamma=5/3$); the cork bullet just slides out when the inside pressure exceeds $P_{cr}$, with outside pressure $P_0$. Now the bullet is launched by pushing the plunger in rapidly, so no heat is exchanged with the gas (adiabatic compression). Find the length of the gas column at the instant the bullet just starts to move, in terms of $r_c$, $T_0$, $L_0$, $P_0$, $P_{cr}$.
solution: A rapid compression with no heat exchanged is adiabatic: $PV^{\gamma}=\mathrm{const}$, with $\gamma=5/3$ for a monatomic ideal gas. Since $V=\pi r_c^2 L$, the relation becomes $P_0L_0^{\gamma}=P_{cr}L^{\gamma}$. The bullet starts to move at the instant the gas pressure reaches $P_{cr}$, so $L=L_0\left(P_0/P_{cr}\right)^{1/\gamma}=L_0\left(P_0/P_{cr}\right)^{3/5}$. Because $P_{cr}>P_0$ the gas column is compressed ($L<L_0$), which is physically sensible; the radius $r_c$ cancels from the adiabatic relation.
hint: Use the adiabatic pressure–volume relation for a monatomic gas and note that the volume is proportional to the gas column length.

question: A cylinder of ideal monatomic gas ($C_V=\tfrac{3}{2}R$) holds a moveable piston; initially the gas is at $P_0$, $V_0$. It is heated at constant volume until the pressure reaches $32P_0$; the piston is then released and the gas expands adiabatically (no heat exchanged) until the pressure returns to $P_0$; finally it is cooled at constant pressure back to the original temperature. Find the maximum volume $V_{\max}$ reached, in terms of $V_0$.
solution: The expansion stroke is adiabatic and (piston released, slow) quasi-static, so $PV^\gamma=\text{const}$. For a monatomic gas $C_V=\tfrac{3}{2}R$, so $C_p=C_V+R=\tfrac{5}{2}R$ and $\gamma=C_p/C_V=5/3$. Applying $P V^{\gamma}$ between $(32P_0,V_0)$ and $(P_0,V_{\max})$: $32P_0\,V_0^{5/3}=P_0\,V_{\max}^{5/3}$, hence $V_{\max}^{5/3}=32\,V_0^{5/3}$ and $V_{\max}=32^{3/5}V_0=(2^5)^{3/5}V_0=8V_0$. Limiting check: a large pressure drop at fixed $\gamma$ must give a large volume increase, and $8>1$ is consistent with expansion during the pressure fall from $32P_0$ to $P_0$.
hint: The unheated expansion is adiabatic; use $PV^\gamma=$ const with the monatomic value of $\gamma$.

question: A monatomic ideal gas ($C_V=\tfrac{3}{2}R$) runs the cycle: isochoric heating from $(P_0,V_0)$ to $(32P_0,V_0)$; adiabatic expansion to $(P_0,V_{\max})$ with $V_{\max}=8V_0$; isobaric cooling at $P_0$ back to $(P_0,V_0)$. In terms of $P_0$ and $V_0$, determine the heat ADDED to the gas during a complete cycle.
solution: Heat enters only on the constant-volume stroke: the adiabatic stroke has $Q=0$ by definition, and the final isobaric stroke cools the gas ($Q<0$). At fixed volume the gas does no work, so by the first law $Q=\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T$. With $PV=nRT$, $n\Delta T=V\Delta P/R$, so $Q_{\text{in}}=\tfrac{3}{2}V_0(32P_0-P_0)=\tfrac{3}{2}(31\,P_0V_0)=\tfrac{93}{2}P_0V_0\approx 46.5\,P_0V_0$. Units: $P_0V_0$ is an energy (J) since $P\,V$ = (N/m$^2$)$\cdot$m$^3$ = N$\cdot$m.
hint: Only one stroke takes in heat; at constant volume, $Q=\Delta U=\frac{3}{2}V\,\Delta P$.

question: A monatomic ideal gas ($C_V=\tfrac{3}{2}R$) runs the cycle: isochoric heating from $(P_0,V_0)$ to $(32P_0,V_0)$; adiabatic expansion to $(P_0,8V_0)$; isobaric cooling at $P_0$ from $8V_0$ back to $V_0$. In terms of $P_0$ and $V_0$, determine the heat REMOVED from the gas during a complete cycle.
solution: Heat leaves only during the final isobaric compression at $P_0$, using $V_{\max}=8V_0$ from the previous part. At constant pressure $Q=nC_p\Delta T=\tfrac{5}{2}P\,\Delta V$ for a monatomic gas ($C_p=\tfrac{5}{2}R$). The volume change is $V_0-8V_0=-7V_0$, so $Q_{\text{out}}=\tfrac{5}{2}P_0(7V_0)=\tfrac{35}{2}P_0V_0=17.5\,P_0V_0$. Consistency check with the first law: the adiabatic work is $-\Delta U=\tfrac{3}{2}(32-8)P_0V_0=36P_0V_0$, the isobaric work is $P_0(V_0-8V_0)=-7P_0V_0$, so $W_{\text{net}}=29P_0V_0$, which must equal $Q_{\text{in}}-Q_{\text{out}}=46.5-17.5=29\,P_0V_0$. $\checkmark$
hint: Use $Q=\frac{5}{2}P\,\Delta V$ on the isobaric stroke with $V_{\max}=8V_0$.

question: For the cycle of the previous parts (isochoric heating with $Q_{\text{in}}=\tfrac{93}{2}P_0V_0$, adiabatic expansion, isobaric cooling with $Q_{\text{out}}=\tfrac{35}{2}P_0V_0$), what is the efficiency of the cycle?
solution: Efficiency is $\eta=W_{\text{net}}/Q_{\text{in}}$. Over a full cycle $\Delta U=0$, so $W_{\text{net}}=Q_{\text{in}}-Q_{\text{out}}=\tfrac{93}{2}P_0V_0-\tfrac{35}{2}P_0V_0=29\,P_0V_0$ (equal to the enclosed area of the $PV$ loop). Thus $\eta=29/(93/2)=58/93\approx0.624$. Sanity checks: $\eta<1$ as required by the second law, and the result is dimensionless and independent of the amount of gas or $V_0$ -- only the pressure ratio 32 and $\gamma=5/3$ matter.
hint: Net work equals heat in minus heat out over one cycle; divide by the heat input only.

question: A planet of radius $R$ made of uniform material generates net power $P$ by radioactive decay, and the heat flows steadily to the surface. The thermal conductivity $k$ of the material is constant. Assuming the surface radiates as a blackbody (emissivity 1) with no radiation incident on it, find the surface temperature $T_s$ in terms of $P$, $R$, and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$.
solution: In steady state the interior temperature profile is time-independent, so ALL the generated power $P$ must pass through the surface and be radiated away (conduction delivers exactly $P$ to the surface; nothing accumulates). The Stefan-Boltzmann law for a blackbody sphere of area $4\pi R^2$ gives $P=4\pi R^2\sigma T_s^4$. Solving, $T_s=(P/4\pi R^2\sigma)^{1/4}$. Dimensional check: $P/(R^2\sigma)$ has units $\text{W}/(\text{m}^2\cdot\text{W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4})=\text{K}^4$, and the fourth root gives kelvin. Limiting check: bigger planets radiate from larger area, so $T_s\propto R^{-1/2}$ for fixed $P$.
hint: In steady state the radiated power equals the internally generated power; use $P=\sigma A T^4$ with $A=4\pi R^2$.

question: A planet of radius $R$ generates power $P$ uniformly throughout its volume; its thermal conductivity $k$ is constant and the heat flow is steady and radial. Find the temperature difference $\Delta T$ between the center and the surface of the planet. (This part is independent of the surface blackbody temperature.)
solution: Apply the conduction law $P_{\text{through}}=kA\,|dT/dx|$ to a sphere of radius $r$ inside the planet. Only the fraction $r^3/R^3$ of the volume lies inside, so the steady power crossing that sphere is $P(r)=P\,r^3/R^3$, flowing through area $A=4\pi r^2$: $P r^3/R^3=-k(4\pi r^2)\,dT/dr$. Hence $dT/dr=-Pr/(4\pi kR^3)$; the growing generated power is exactly cancelled by the growing area, so the gradient grows linearly with $r$. Integrating from center to surface: $T_c-T_s=\int_0^R \dfrac{Pr\,dr}{4\pi kR^3}=\dfrac{PR^2}{8\pi kR^3}=\dfrac{P}{8\pi kR}$. Units: $\text{W}/(\text{W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{m})=\text{K}$. $\checkmark$
hint: Only the heat generated interior to radius $r$ crosses radius $r$; combine that with $kA\,dT/dr$ and integrate.

question: A potato gun fires a potato horizontally along a cylinder of cross-sectional area $A$ with one closed end. At firing the potato is at rest, the gas trapped between the closed end and the potato has volume $V_0$ and pressure $P_0>P_{atm}$, and atmospheric pressure $P_{atm}$ acts on the potato's front face. The gas is diatomic ($C_v=5R/2$, $C_p=7R/2$, so $\gamma=7/5$); the potato moves fast enough that no heat enters the gas, friction and leaks are negligible, and the expansion is quasi-static and adiabatic. The barrel length $L$ may be varied. Find the maximum kinetic energy $E_{max}$ with which the potato can exit the barrel, in terms of $P_0$, $P_{atm}$, $V_0$.
solution: The adiabatic expansion obeys $P=P_0(V_0/V)^{\gamma}$ with $\gamma=7/5$, and the potato's kinetic energy is the net work $E(V_f)=\int_{V_0}^{V_f}(P-P_{atm})\,dV=\frac{P_0V_0-P_0V_0^{\gamma}V_f^{1-\gamma}}{\gamma-1}-P_{atm}(V_f-V_0)$. Setting $\frac{dE}{dV_f}=P_f-P_{atm}=0$: the maximum occurs when the gas has expanded exactly to atmospheric pressure — beyond that the net force reverses and slows the potato.
